title: Traffic Pattern — drag labels onto the diagram
status: 2 questions covering Part 3's fourth competency, 'Identifying the parts of a standard traffic pattern (e.g., upwind, crosswind, etc.)': one on the five LEGS, one on the four TURNS between them. Both use the same left-hand RWY 27/09 artwork and disjoint zone sets.
source: VictorOne English Phraseology Exam Briefing Package 1 (Part 3, competency 4). The five LEG names come from the 'Left-hand pattern' diagram in 'A Guide to VFR Phraseology' (Karmen Stumberger, MSc), section 5 'Traffic circuit and landing', printed p. 21 — they appear in the guide ONLY as labels drawn inside that picture, and the guide nowhere defines what any leg is. The four TURN names are NOT in the guide at any point; they are included on the exam authority's instruction (the real exam tests them), and their explanation therefore teaches the turns rather than merely confirming them. Printed page = PDF page - 2.
authoring_notes:
R1 LEGS AND TURNS ARE SEPARATE QUESTIONS, over disjoint zone sets. The artwork carries 9 drop zones: 5 legs at canonical indices 0,2,4,6,8 and 4 turns at 1,3,5,7. DIAG-01 asks for the legs, DIAG-02 for the turns, and each delivers only its own zones — the DB requires answer.length === zones.length, so a question cannot ship a zone it does not ask about. The other set's labels remain in the shared chip pool as distractors, which is what makes each question discriminating.

R1a SOURCE ASYMMETRY, STATED PLAINLY. The leg names are in the guide's diagram; the turn names are not in the guide at all. DIAG-02 therefore tests vocabulary the student's preparation material never supplies, and it exists because the exam authority says the real exam asks for it. Its explanation must TEACH the four turns — where each sits and which two legs it joins — not just restate the answer. An earlier revision of this file made the opposite ruling ('five legs only, turns are distractors, never answers'); it was reversed on that authority, and the reversal is recorded here rather than silently overwritten so nobody re-derives the old rule from the guide alone.

R2 IDS ARE NOT AUTHORED. Zones and labels come from the shared layout module (rwy-2709-layout.ts) so drop targets always match the drawn artwork; ids are derived — zone from (image_ref, canonical index), label from its own text — so no author can encode the zone-to-label pairing. This closed a real defect: the previous hand-written label ids had strictly ascending second characters in canonical order, so sorting the delivered label ids restored the answer key. `answer_by_zone` maps a canonical zone index to a label TEXT; the importer resolves both to derived ids.

R3 WHY NO MORE THAN TWO QUESTIONS. The guide contains exactly one pattern diagram, for a left-hand circuit ('The examples in this section refer to the left-hand pattern'). A right-hand variant needs new artwork, which is engineering, not authoring. Subdividing either set further — three legs here, two there — would test less while appearing to test more.

R4 THE QUESTION MAY NOT DEPEND ON A DEFINITION THE SOURCE LACKS. The guide never says what 'base' means, only where it is drawn, so both questions ask the student to place names on a picture. Explanations teach after the answer is revealed and may go further.
grading_notes: Graded as a pure set comparison by check_non_mc_answer: every zone must carry its canonical label. Delivered by get_quiz_questions with the answer map stripped and the label pool shuffled; zones are delivered in stored order.

questions.prompt: This is a standard left-hand traffic pattern. Drag each name onto the leg it belongs to.
questions.explanation:
**The five legs of the circuit, in the order you fly them.** After take-off you climb straight ahead on the **upwind** leg, along the extended runway centreline. You then turn left onto **crosswind**, perpendicular to the runway. The **downwind** leg runs parallel to the runway in the opposite direction to landing — this is where you make your compulsory downwind report, and where the controller will usually sequence you against other traffic. Turning left again puts you on **base**, perpendicular once more, and the last left turn rolls you onto **final approach**, lined up with the runway.

**Why left?** In a left-hand pattern every turn is to the left. The guide notes that a left-hand pattern is the default and needs no announcement, while a right-hand circuit must be specified — you will hear *report right downwind* rather than plain *report downwind*.

**Two reports are compulsory:** downwind and final. Everything else — base, for example — is made on request, which is why you will often hear *report base* from the controller rather than volunteering it.

**The four turns between these legs are asked for separately.** Here they appear only as distractor chips — placing 'Crosswind turn' on a leg is the mistake this question is built to catch.

questions.prompt: Same left-hand traffic pattern. Drag each name onto the turn it belongs to.
questions.explanation:
**Each turn is named for the leg you are turning ONTO, not the one you are leaving.** That single rule answers all four, and it is the only thing you need to carry into the exam.

Leaving the upwind leg and rolling out perpendicular to the runway, you have joined crosswind — so that is the **crosswind turn**. From crosswind onto the leg running parallel and opposite to the landing direction is the **downwind turn**. From downwind onto the perpendicular leg before final is the **base turn**. And the last one, rolling out aligned with the runway, is the **final turn**.

In a left-hand pattern all four are to the left, which is why the circuit direction only ever needs announcing when it is right-hand — you will hear *report right downwind*, never *report left downwind*.

The five legs are the subject of the companion question; here they are distractors. Watch the **final turn** in particular: it is the turn, while *final approach* is the straight leg that follows it, and they are easy to confuse under time pressure.
